subject: chemistry-2
question: In a model of extracellular fluid, the bicarbonate-to-dissolved-CO2 ratio falls from 20:1 to 10:1 while the pKa remains 6.1. What would happen to the pH?

options.text: It rises from about 7.4 to about 7.7
It stays near 7.4 because the pKa did not change
It falls from about 7.4 to about 7.1
It falls from about 7.4 to about 6.4

explanation:
Using pH = pKa + log([HCO3-]/[CO2]), the 20:1 ratio gives 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4, while the 10:1 ratio gives 6.1 + 1 = 7.1. Halving the ratio lowers pH by log 2, about 0.3 unit, not a full unit, because the relationship is logarithmic. Option D would require a 2:1 ratio and option A would require the ratio to increase rather than fall.

ELI-10: In the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation only the ratio of the two buffer members, not their absolute amounts, sets the pH once the pKa is fixed. Because the ratio enters as a logarithm, cutting it in half subtracts log 2, which is about 0.3 unit. That is why a pH of 7.1 can arise either from losing bicarbonate or from retaining CO2: both change the same ratio, and 0.3 unit is already a large clinical move.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
